newsitem.title: USA: Clinton attacks fashion industry's "heroin chic".
newsitem.headline: Clinton attacks fashion industry's "heroin chic".

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday criticised the fashion industry for promoting the allure of heroin in its sales pitch to young people, saying it was wrong to "glamorize addiction to sell clothes."
Speaking at the White House to a forum on drug abuse held by the U.S. Conference of Mayors, Clinton censured the fashion industry for "increasing the allure of heroin among young people."

"We now see on college campuses and in neighbourhoods heroin becoming increasingly the drug of choice," Clinton told the mayors. "And we know that part of this has to do with the images that are finding their way to our young people.

"Our society cannot say on the one hand we want to have a tough, intolerant attitude toward drugs and on the other hand send a very different message every time there might be a little money to be made on it."
He was attacking so-called heroin chic, promoted by some fashion photography showing models posed as if they were under the influence of drugs.
The trend has been prominent in recent years in fashion magazines and advertising campaigns by the industry featuring gaunt models who appeared to be in a stupor.
Clinton praised some industry leaders for "admitting flat-out that images projected in fashion photos in the last few years have made heroin addiction seem glamorous and sexy and cool."
"As some of the people in those images start to die now, it becomes obvious that that is not true," Clinton said. "You do not need to glamorize addiction to sell clothes."
Patrick McCarthy, chairman and editorial director of W magazine, a monthly women's fashion magazine, and Women's Wear Daily, the bible of the fashion industry, said he welcomed the president's views.
"I think some people went overboard, and you can't condemn the whole industry for it," he said. "The good thing about this is more people are aware of it."

"Very few people go out and decide to do an ad campaign or a photo layout encouraging people to take heroin. They don't do it deliberately, but people got carried away by the glamour of decadence," he said. "And editors were not paying enough attention, and art designers were not paying enough attention."
"The result was a number of stories that did, in fact, glamourize drug use and the pursuit of decadence as a lifestyle," he said.

White House officials said Clinton's comments were prompted in part by a New York Times article this week on the death of Davide Sorrenti, a 20-year-old fashion photographer whose work often captured a "heroin look."
His death in February from a drug overdose has led to soul-searching in the trendy world of fashion and the publications that cover it.
"American fashion has been an enormous source of creativity and beauty and art and, frankly, economic prosperity for the United States," Clinton said.

"But the glorification of heroin is not creative. It's destructive. It's not beautiful. It is ugly. And this is not about art. It's about life and death. And glorifying death is not good for any society," he said.
Although Clinton has been promoting his administration's anti-drug efforts, the speech marked the first time he has singled out the fashion industry for criticism.
The music industry and Hollywood moviemakers have been criticised in the past, prompting leaders in both fields to increase efforts to stop the glamorous portrayal of drug use.
Barbara Lippert, advertising columnist for New York magazine, said the president should not blame just the fashion industry.

"It's always simplistic to blame one area," she said. "It's the whole culture of youth. It's movies and books and videos and music and commercials, not just fashion. It's very simplistic to point fingers."
